rationale: Attempted the next increment - configuration events aimed at an existing serving member (so a voter can be demoted and re-promoted) - and it failed in a way worth recording rather than hiding. With application lag present, aiming a JointImplicit change at a serving member made the harness panic with 'config is already joint' inside applyConfChange: a node applies a joint-entering change while its own tracked configuration is still joint, because the auto-leave it should have applied first is exactly the kind of entry the lag event holds back. That is the target's documented contract for an invalid configuration change (the application must apply each change in the order its log provides, and a change that enters joint while joint is invalid), so the failure is a harness modelling error, not a target defect: the harness applied a change out of the order the contract assumes at that node. I reverted to the last known-good revision (configuration events aimed at the joining node 4 only, JointImplicit half the time, lag, restarts, witness) and confirmed locally that it runs again and reproduces the executed counters exactly (elections=470, proposals=461, conf_change_proposals=262, restarts=429, unapplied_conf_change_states=48, stalled_states=0, violations=0), so no experiment is requested this turn. The failure does open a real, sourced follow-up worth pursuing next: with Config.DisableConfChangeValidation left at its default, the leader's propose-time check is explicitly best-effort against its own possibly stale configuration, so a joint-entering change can enter the log while some lagging node is still joint; the question is whether a permitted sequence can leave a node unable to apply a committed change except by panicking, i.e. whether the lag/demotion ordering is bounded by application duties alone or by anything the target enforces.

investigations.question: The failure observed while building the sweep's demotion event was 'config is already joint' from applyConfChange, raised when a node with application lag applied a joint-entering ChangeNodes entry while its own tracker was still joint because the leave-joint entry preceding it had not been applied yet. Which permitted histories can put a committed joint-entering configuration change behind an unapplied leave-joint entry at the same node, how does the leader's propose-time validation interact with that (Config.DisableConfChangeValidation defaults to false, and the code documents the check as best-effort against a possibly stale configuration, with both false positives and false negatives), and what does the target require of the application to avoid the panic - strictly in-order application of its own log, or something stronger about what may be proposed while a joint configuration is in flight?
investigations.hypothesis: The panic is the documented consequence of an application that applies committed entries out of order or of a proposal that the leader's best-effort check allowed through while its configuration was stale; the target's own duty is only that the application applies entries in log order, so a permitted history exists in which a node is forced to apply a joint-entering change while joint, and the question is whether the propose-time check (or the auto-leave path) bounds it in every case.
investigations.discriminator: Build a three-voter cluster with AutoLeave/JointImplicit, hold one follower's application back (so its leave-joint entry stays unapplied while the leader is non-joint again), propose a second joint-entering change, and observe whether the withheld follower, once its application catches up in log order, applies a joint-entering change while its tracker is joint - and whether the leader's propose-time validation had refused or rewritten that change. Compare with the control where the follower's application keeps up.
